good evening three weeks have now passed since the last board meeting since then some important progress has been made, and I want to acknowledge that. But many families do not see this as closure because what many of us have struggled with has never just been about outcomes. It is also about what happened along the way and making sure it does not happen again. These concerns are not abstract. They look like this. One student became so distraught that he wandered alone around the sport fields until someone from the athletic staff found him. Other students learned about disciplinary decisions through rumors, while some parents first learned through a district-wide email, neither directly from the school. In my own child's case, the written notice stated four days, yet he was kept home for five days. We made the school aware that we had never received the notice, but despite opportunities to correct it, the additional day still occurred. These are only a few examples. Every family has a story like this. These are not technicalities. These are basic responsibilities. A distraught child wandering school grounds alone is not a technicality. A child missing an additional day of school because a breakdown in process was never corrected is not a technicality. These situations had real emotional impacts on children and raised real safety concerns as well. Student well-being felt secondary, not central. This is not the Irvington way, and I believe we can do better. I'm not here to destroy administrators or suggest children should avoid accountability. They should not. I'm here because they are children, and how adults respond to them matters. What our community is asking is simple. Recognition that things went wrong, meaningful reflection on what happened, and corrective action to prevent it from happening again. So what could that look like? It begins with three areas deserving closer examination. First, three weeks ago, members of this community stood here and spoke openly about how inflaming the superintendent's communication felt. In the weeks since, many families continue to feel hurt and unheard. The lack of public follow-up has been disappointing given how public this was from the start. When concerns as serious as hate speech are raised in a community, families deserve the conversation not to end with the initial message, but to continue with reflection and a path forward. Second, reflection should include looking at both how decisions were made and how they were carried out. Families remain concerned about whether the decision to suspend reflected thoughtful judgment and individualized consideration and why important procedures were not followed. Both matter because consequences should teach and support growth and the processes that guide them should be followed consistently. And finally, I ask this board to conduct a meaningful review of what happened and to share with the community what was learned. I respect the work you do and believe the board can lead that review. Impacted families would welcome the opportunity to be part of the conversation. I'll be honest. I am angry. many families are, but anger alone improves nothing. What matters is what we do. Speaking openly about failures is how improvement begins. We are not here to simply point out what went wrong. We want to help make it better so that no child or family should go through this again.
